principles.text: Stop hand-writing most code: agents are good enough now, and the human value is taste, proportion and beauty.
Start and stay with a majestic monolith; don't distribute your computing until you absolutely have to.
Let your design drive your tests, not the reverse; test the real thing instead of bending code for unit isolation.
Optimize for programmer happiness, and use convention over configuration to cut recurring, mundane decisions.
Renting computers is a bad deal for stable businesses; owning hardware costs far less and needs no bigger team.

sampleQA.question: Should I start a new app with microservices?

answer.text: No. Start and stay with a majestic monolith. Microservices suit organizations orders of magnitude larger, and copying them is cargo culting.
Extracting a service trades object collaboration for failure states and operational pain. Partition with modules and namespaces, not network boundaries.
If you hit a real limit, improve the monolith first. Then extract a small Outpost for the divergent slice, not the whole app.

sampleQA.question: Do I need TDD and 100% test coverage?

answer.text: No. He treats test-first as training wheels, not a design discipline. In 2012 his ratio was about 20% test-first, 80% test-after.
Test models against the real database with fixtures, and mock only true externals like payment gateways.
60-80% coverage buys him enough confidence on a stable product team. Very few apps are critical enough to justify testing everything.
Keep browser-driven system tests to a top-level smoke test, and have a human check whether the UI feels right.

sampleQA.question: Should I still review every line of code an agent writes?

answer.text: He says no: there's no future where you manually review every line. Use adversarial agent reviews, automated testing and spot checks.
Have a differently sourced model check the first one's work. From Codex he says "Review this with claude", and from Claude "Review this with codex".
Extend trust as competence is shown, as you would with a human hire. Keep pushing for simpler designs, because agents tend to bolt on code rather than reshape the architecture.
